chapter: Ensemble, harmony and the Ory band
title: Harmony in the band: Oliver and Jelly Roll arrangements
summary: Asked about harmony, DeVore discusses breaks and harmonized parts in the Oliver band and the polished Ory band with Mutt Carey.

blocks.x: What's the place of harmony in a band?

Well, now you, this is a pretty involved thing. You see now, the bands that are playing today are, if you were looking over the whole history of New Orleans music, these are the seconds, so to speak. The real top notch professional New Orleans men had everything these guys did besides working on arrangements like the Oliver Band for instance. They say the Oliver Band down here must have really been something. A lot more fluid than the band that recorded in Chicago. But if you listen to that band in Chicago, they had tunes that had two or three different strains. Breaks. You see, Jelly Roll knew more about it than anybody. He was a guy at that time that understood what was going on. I think Joe did too, but Jelly really did. And it's the breaks that mean so much. And for harmonies, well you listen to Working Man Blues by Oliver Band. And every band is playing a different part at the same time harmonized out. You can hear the two horns. Louie is playing a harmonic part underneath the lead. The trombone player has this part. The clarinet player has this part. And we do a lot of that. We call it three part, very basic three part harmonies. Ori's band. Now there's a band, the classic Ori band, the one with Papa Mutt. And two or three of the good clarinet players. Orma Simeon or Darnell Howard. And Ori, with that wonderful rhythm section. I think that band probably, of the modern bands, came as close as being the real polished New Orleans. With the same amount, the roughness was still there, but the organization was as polished as any band.
